answer: A practical defense is to require each agent to lock a nontrivial stake in a vault before it can submit jobs or earn reputation. The protocol caps voting and rewards by stake-weighted influence, then slashes the bond when independent audits prove collusion or fabricated work. Creating identities is still possible, but each useful identity ties up capital and risks forfeiture, so splitting one attacker across many names does not multiply influence for free. Basalt-backed contracts can make the rule durable, while velvet onboarding keeps legitimate entry accessible.
